faq.q: How does shivering warm you up?
faq.a: Shivering is rapid, involuntary muscle contraction. Muscles release heat whenever they work, and because shivering muscles do no useful movement, almost all the energy they use becomes heat.
asks: Tell me about muscles twitching fast

faq.q: What tells your body to shiver?
faq.a: The hypothalamus in the brain monitors skin and blood temperature. When the body gets too cold, it sends nerve signals that trigger shivering.
asks: Tell me about the thermostat reacting

faq.q: Why do teeth chatter in the cold?
faq.a: The jaw muscles shiver along with the rest, contracting and relaxing quickly, so the teeth knock together.
asks: Why do my teeth rattle when I am cold?

faq.q: What else does the body do to keep warm?
faq.a: Blood vessels in the skin narrow so less heat escapes, hairs stand up giving goosebumps, and the body can burn more fuel in special brown fat, especially in babies.
asks: How does the body save heat?

faq.q: Can you stop shivering by trying?
faq.a: Only a little, briefly. Shivering is controlled automatically by the brain, so it carries on until you are warm enough.

facts: Shivering can increase the body's heat production several times over the resting level.
The hypothalamus controls shivering as part of body temperature regulation.
